title.en: Beatles and Beach Boys pushing formal borders
title.zh: 尝试拓宽音乐边界的Beatles与Beach Boys

summary.en: After huge commercial success, the Beatles and the Beach Boys began treating the studio as an instrument and exploring how to widen music’s borders.
summary.zh: 在获得了巨大的商业成功后，Beatles与Beach Boys开始尝试将录音室作为乐器，探索扩宽音乐边界的可能

body.zh:
在获得了巨大的商业成功后，Beatles与Beach Boys开始尝试将录音室作为乐器，探索扩宽音乐边界的可能

在前几章中，我们介绍了Beatles和Beach Boys的音乐，现在我们继续这个话题。这两个乐队不仅有相同的听众群体，而且都隶属于洛杉矶的Capitol唱片公司（至少在美国是这样的）。当时Beatles在英国和EMI唱片签了一份对他们来说很重要的合约，但是在美国，他们和Beach Boys隶属同一家唱片公司，也就是洛杉矶的Capitol唱片公司。他们的共同点不仅在于同样的听众和厂牌，还在于他们都对自己的音乐充满野心，准备开始挑战作为音乐人的极限——尽管这些特点有时可能会被忽略。之前我们讲到Beatles和Beach Boys的时候，曾涉及过这一点，现在我们接着以前的内容讲，来为他们之后的迷幻音乐家们的出现做铺垫。

Beatles和Beach Boys这两支乐队都在探索新的可能，他们优秀的唱片销量使得他们拥有了整天待在录音棚里工作的自由——当时的录音棚是个花销巨大的地方，唱片公司不可能让他们旗下的艺人成天待在录音棚，因为公司的目标十分明确：投入必须带来经济回报。而这两个乐队还在继续突破已知的极限，他们都把录音棚当做是一种作曲的工具，用来探索在录音棚里进行创作的可能，以及音乐中新的立场、新的声音。他们都选择在音乐中加入古典元素，从19世纪的传统和先锋艺术(Avant-garde) 中汲取灵感。在此，我们可以讲讲在他们歌曲中的管弦乐器，以及磁带剪辑、磁带循环的广泛运用。这些东西你在Beatles和Beach Boys的音乐中都能找到。

现在我们来讲讲Beach Boys的音乐，以及其在60年代中期 (约1967年) 以来是如何变得野心勃勃的。在1965年初的时候，乐队主唱Brian Wilson因为不适应坐飞机不再和乐队一起巡演，而是在录音棚里担任全职工作。于是乐队其他成员在巡演的时候，他就待在家里，并得以享受待在录音棚的奢侈。因为Beach Boys的唱片销量可观，他可以随时预约录音棚，坐在那儿做些新鲜的尝试。Brian Wilson和当时洛杉矶最顶尖的录音棚音乐人The Wrecking Crew合作。这个团体并不单指一个乐队，而是由12名左右顶尖的录音棚音乐人组成。Brian Wilson制作各种各样的音乐，这些音乐人也参与其中。他们发行过一部专辑《Pet Sounds》的4CD珍藏套装，除了专辑的正式部分以外，其余全都是为制作那一张总共只有35分钟的专辑准备的素材，这些素材还只是挑选出来的一部分而已。我想说的是，Brian Wilson录制了不少东西，做了不少尝试，也许我们可以在他《California Girls》这首歌中感受到这一点。这首歌我们之前也提到过，不过在1966年中期发布的运用了更多实验性艺术形式的《Pet Sounds》才是他们真正的大作。这张专辑受到1965年末Beatles发行的专辑《Rubber Soul》的影响。也许《Pet Sounds》中有两首歌可以印证他们当时的野心：一首是《Wouldn't It Be Nice》，另一首是《God Only Knows》——后者尤其明显。接着，在1966年他们又制作了《Good Vibrations》 这首单曲在Beatles的《Revolver》之后发行，也就是1966年8月。在《Good Vibrations》的音轨里，你能很清楚地听到 Brian Wilson 准备了不同素材，然后把它们以某种方式剪辑在一起，合成出一种迷幻的感觉。

现在我们来讲讲1966年下半年 Brian打算发行的名叫《Smile》的专辑。这张唱片甚至打出了定在1967年发行的广告，但后来了无音讯。或许是当时录音棚里做的音乐太多，又或是他们沉迷于迷幻剂，总之这张专辑最终没有完成。同样在1967年，Beatles发行了双面单曲《Penny Lane》和《Strawberry Fields》，而 Beach Boys 在《Smile》制作失败后于1967年8月发行了《Smiley Smile》取而代之，这张专辑的发行正好是在1967年6月的《Sgt. Pepper》发行之后。我们比较这两支乐队所发行的专辑，可以看到他们的野心都越来越大。 我猜Brian Wilson在这次竞争中有些丧气，因为他没能把《Smile》这张专辑做出来（虽然近几年它已经录制好了）。我在几章前讲过这件事，这张唱片很不错，有自己的特色，如果它能在那时候如愿发行的话，反响应该会很大，但它并没有发行。你可以认为这两个乐队间的来来往往是一种友好的竞争——但也许从Beatles那一方来说稍微友好一点，而从Brian Wilson的角度看来就很难说了。

让我们再来看看Beatles。在1966年8月发行的《Revolver》毫无疑问为Beatles的音乐中注入了一些迷幻的元素，这主要是因为这张唱片里的最后一首歌《Tomorrow Never Knows》——它无疑是当时Beatles发行的最前卫、最有试验性也是最具野心的一首歌。像我之前讲的那样，这首歌是继《Penny Lane》和《Strawberry Fields》之后发行的，这两首歌原先是作为概念专辑的一部分。在当时，也就是1966年8月19日，他们决定不再巡演 ，而只担任录音棚乐队，因此这张专辑的制作就可以完全不用担心表演的因素，他们就可以毫无顾忌地尝试录音棚里的任何东西。《Penny Lane》和《Strawberry Fields》原本打算要收录在这张讲述在利物浦的成长经历的概念专辑里，但由于这两首歌已经收录在《Magical Mystery Tours》里，因此他们不想在以后的专辑中再放进这两首歌。新专辑取名为《Sgt. Pepper's Lonely Hearts Club Band》，在这张专辑里，Beatles实际上成为了 Sgt. Pepper's Lonely Hearts Club乐队，他们会对外宣称我们是Sgt. Pepper's Lonely Hearts Club乐队。这张专辑采用了前后曲目接续的形式。在专辑开头你会首先听到他们在《Sgt. Pepper's Lonely Hearts Club》这首歌曲的最后说，下面由Billy Shears演唱（其实也就是Ringo），于是就接着演唱《With A Little Help From My Friends》。不过到了下一首歌他们就放弃了这种形式，只是一首一首歌地播放，直到正面专辑末尾又重复了《Sgt. Pepper》里的音乐，然后就接上了专辑反面的第一首歌《A Day In The Life》。这张专辑采用了特殊的包装创意，它的外层封套是折叠式的，打开后是乐队成员的照片，当你把专辑从外层专辑套中抽出来之后，可以看到里面有印着胡须和臂章的纸板片，你可以把他们剪下来戴在身上。专辑里的花样确实不少，封面后页就印着所有歌词——这在今天并不罕见，但那是第一张把歌词印在封面后页的流行乐唱片，这样你就可以不用听歌也知道歌词了。Bob Dylan作为一个重量级的词作者，我们讲过的他所有专辑都没有像这样把歌词印在专辑包装外侧的，因此这算是一个让歌词内容解放的创举。这张专辑也是第一张概念专辑——但就算没人对此提出质疑，这可能也不是历史上第一张概念专辑。概念专辑这个理念可以追溯到摇滚乐诞生之前的Frank Sinatra或者爵士歌手John Coltrane时期。但即便如此，它还是凭着Sgt. Pepper 乐队这个创意被认为是第一张概念专辑。John Lennon 总是说，“我的歌本可以出现在所有 Beatles 的专辑里，我其实不懂 Sgt. Pepper 这个创意是什么意思，我的歌跟它一点关系都没有”。但是John说了什么并不重要，重要的是人们对这张专辑的看法，因为Beatles已经在模仿想象中的Sgt. Pepper乐队了，他们在模仿概念专辑里表达的东西，这也是这张专辑如此有影响力的原因。专辑里面最有野心、最会用音乐说话的歌也许就是《Being for the Benefit of Mr. Kite》了，因为其中用到了磁带循环。但是专辑的最后一首《A Day in the Life》则在很多人编写摇滚乐编年史时被赞为“史诗般的五分钟”。在这首歌里，其中有两处变调完全是即兴的——那些管弦乐手可以即兴演奏自己的乐器，只要在某个特定的时间点一起奏鸣达到乐句渐强的高潮部分就可以了。我保证如果你听过这首歌，你肯定知道我的意思：所有的东西都拼接到了一起。Johh唱开头段，Paul唱中间段，接着又是John的部分。这些片段放被到一起，做出了一种渐强乐团赞美诗的效果。这些元素使得这首歌成为了那时候为止他们最伟大的一首歌，也为后来的追随他们音乐人们树立了榜样，提高了标准。他们试图在1967年12月发行的《Magical Mystery Tour》延续这个想法，还为此制作了同名电影，但这部电影失败了——大多数人都对此评价不高。他们乐意看到Beatles，听到他们的音乐，但是觉得电影却不怎么样。彼时那些记者们终于可以说Beatles也干了件彻底失败的事——当然我们都知道他们本身并不失败，但是1967年到1968年，媒体还是想写那么一个故事，说Beatles完蛋了，他们终于干出了一件彻底失败的事。《Magical Mystery Tour》里包括了《I Am the Walrus》的录像。 Paul McCartney好几次都说到过他不同意这么做。也就是在1967年的8月，他们自1962年以来一直合作的经纪人Brian Epstein因为吸毒过量过世了，这导致Beatles在后来一段时间内一直没有经纪人。那段时间乐队沉浸在印度教和超验主义 (transcendental) 的冥想中。由此我们可以看出关于 Beatles职业生涯的两件事：其一，是他们碰到了管理上的问题需要一段时间解决；另外，在此过程中他们也经受了不小的经济损失，但同时这也是他们转向东方文化的时期。

回到《Rubber Soul》这张专辑，我们已经在《Norwegian Wood》这首歌里听过西塔琴 (一种印度乐器) 的声音。George Harrison 对于东方乐器的兴趣在《Sgt. Pepper》专辑中的《Within You Without You》中也有表现。Beatles那时把变体论(Transubstantiation) 加入了表演中，他们去印度跟着印度大师Maharishi)学习冥想，还把这些东西推向了主流。要知道我们在讲Beatles 和 Beach Boys 时，我们讲的是主流艺人，而不是地下的迷幻音乐。在1967年的夏天，作为智慧之源的东方文化与西方文化碰撞交融，另类的精神灵性真正地与他们的音乐融合到了一起。当然了，Beatles也没有继续坚持迷幻音乐而是选择了回头：1968年12月发布的《The White Album》专辑更多地是体现Beatles作为传统词曲作者的一面，他们开始返回去寻找最初的东西。《The White Album》最具有野心的一首歌是 John Lennon 用磁带录制《Revolution 9》，它或许和音乐史上广泛传播的大多数电子音乐 (electronic music) 都不一样。虽说很多人大概只听了这首歌一遍就不听了，甚至都没有听完，不过它让很多人知道了电子音乐还可以是这样的。

本应是《Get Back》的《Let It Be》最终在1969年1月以的面貌发行，这张专辑又回归了他们的本色。1969年9月，Beatles 发行了他们的最后一张专辑《Abbey Road》——大概这张专辑才最称得上是所谓的迷幻音乐。第一面的最后一首歌是《I Want You/ She's So Heavy) 》这首歌的结尾有渐强的噪音以及重复的吉他和弦，最后戛然而止。在第二面Paul把很多片段放在一起使其延伸出了一组歌曲。在这个时期，Beatles和Beach Boys的所作所为在某种程度上为主流注入了更具有野心的音乐元素。

下节课我们将开始学习旧金山的Haight-Ashbury区的迷幻亚文化，以及旧金山广播电台的发展，看看与此同时那里发生的事。
body.en:
After huge commercial success, the Beatles and the Beach Boys began treating the studio as an instrument and exploring how to widen music’s borders.

In earlier chapters we introduced the Beatles’ and Beach Boys’ music; we continue that thread. The two bands shared not only audiences but, at least in the U.S., Los Angeles’s Capitol Records. The Beatles had an important EMI deal in Britain, but in America they and the Beach Boys were on the same label—Capitol in L.A. They shared more than audience and label: both were ambitious about their music and ready to test their limits as musicians—traits sometimes overlooked. We touched this when we covered them before; we pick it up now as setup for the psychedelic musicians who follow.

Both bands explored new possibilities. Strong sales gave them freedom to spend whole days in the studio—then a costly place; labels would not normally let artists live there, because investment had to pay back. These two kept pushing known limits. Both treated the studio as a compositional tool, exploring what could be made there and new stances and sounds in the music. Both added classical elements, drawing on nineteenth-century tradition and the avant-garde. We can talk about orchestral instruments in their songs, and wide use of tape editing and tape loops. You find these in both Beatles and Beach Boys music.

Turn to the Beach Boys and how, from the mid-1960s (around 1967), their music grew ambitious. In early 1965 lead singer Brian Wilson stopped touring because he could not handle flying, and worked full-time in the studio. While the others toured, he stayed home and enjoyed the luxury of studio time. With strong sales he could book the studio anytime and try new things. He worked with L.A.’s top session players, the Wrecking Crew—not one band, but about a dozen elite studio musicians. Brian made all kinds of music with them. A 4-CD Pet Sounds box exists: besides the finished album, the rest is material prepared for that ~35-minute record—and only selected takes. Brian recorded a lot and tried a lot; you can sense that in “California Girls,” which we mentioned before. But the real statement was Pet Sounds in mid-1966, more experimental, influenced by the Beatles’ late-1965 Rubber Soul. Two tracks especially show the ambition: “Wouldn’t It Be Nice” and, above all, “God Only Knows.” Then in 1966 came the single “Good Vibrations,” after the Beatles’ Revolver (August 1966). In “Good Vibrations” you clearly hear Brian preparing different sections and editing them together into a psychedelic feel.

In late 1966 Brian planned an album called Smile. Ads even set a 1967 release; then nothing. Too much studio music, or immersion in psychedelics—anyway it was never finished. Also in 1967 the Beatles released the double A-side “Penny Lane” / “Strawberry Fields Forever”; after Smile failed, the Beach Boys issued Smiley Smile in August 1967 in its place—after Sgt. Pepper in June 1967. Comparing the albums, both bands’ ambition kept growing. I suspect Brian was discouraged in that rivalry because he could not finish Smile (though it has been completed in recent years). I mentioned this a few chapters back: the record is strong and distinctive; had it come out then, the response would have been large—but it did not. You can see a friendly competition between the bands—perhaps friendlier from the Beatles’ side than from Brian’s.

Now the Beatles. August 1966’s Revolver clearly injected psychedelic elements, mainly because of the closing track “Tomorrow Never Knows”—then their most avant-garde, experimental, and ambitious song. As noted earlier, it followed “Penny Lane” and “Strawberry Fields Forever,” originally meant for a concept album. On 19 August 1966 they decided to stop touring and become a studio band only, so album-making need not worry about live performance; they could try anything in the studio. “Penny Lane” and “Strawberry Fields” were meant for a concept album about growing up in Liverpool, but once on Magical Mystery Tour they did not want them on later albums. The new album was titled Sgt. Pepper’s Lonely Hearts Club Band: the Beatles effectively became that band and would say they were Sgt. Pepper’s Lonely Hearts Club Band. Tracks run into each other. At the start, at the end of “Sgt. Pepper’s Lonely Hearts Club Band,” they announce Billy Shears (Ringo) and go into “With a Little Help from My Friends.” Then they drop that device and play song by song until the end of side one reprises Sgt. Pepper music and leads into side two’s first track, “A Day in the Life.” The packaging was special: a gatefold outer sleeve with band photos; inside, cardboard cutouts of mustaches and badges you could wear. Plenty of extras; the back cover printed all the lyrics—common now, but the first pop album to print lyrics on the back so you could read without listening. Bob Dylan, a major songwriter, never put lyrics on the outer package like that on the albums we covered; this was a step that freed lyric content. It is also often called the first concept album—though even if no one challenges that, it may not be history’s first. The idea goes back before rock to Frank Sinatra or jazz singers like John Coltrane. Still, the Sgt. Pepper band conceit made it count as the first concept album in many minds. John Lennon always said his songs could have sat on any Beatles album; he did not really get the Sgt. Pepper idea and his songs had nothing to do with it. What John said matters less than how people heard the album: the Beatles were already imitating an imagined Sgt. Pepper band and what the concept expressed—that is why it was so influential. Perhaps the most ambitious, music-speaking track is “Being for the Benefit of Mr. Kite!” with its tape loops. The closer, “A Day in the Life,” is often praised in rock chronicles as an “epic five minutes.” Two key changes are fully improvised—orchestral players could improvise as long as they hit a shared crescendo climax at a set point. If you have heard it, you know: everything splices together. John sings the opening, Paul the middle, then John again. Fragments are joined into a rising orchestral hymn. These elements made it their greatest song to that point and raised the bar for those who followed. They tried to extend the idea with Magical Mystery Tour in December 1967 and a film of the same name—the film failed; most people liked seeing and hearing the Beatles but not the movie. Journalists could finally say the Beatles had thoroughly flopped—of course they had not, but in 1967–68 the press wanted a story that they were finished. Magical Mystery Tour includes the “I Am the Walrus” footage. Paul McCartney several times said he disagreed with doing it that way. Also in August 1967, manager Brian Epstein, with them since 1962, died of a drug overdose; for a stretch they had no manager. They immersed in Hinduism and transcendental meditation. Two things about their career: management problems that took time to fix; and, while they took financial hits, this was also when they turned toward Eastern culture.

Back to Rubber Soul: we already heard sitar (an Indian instrument) on “Norwegian Wood.” George Harrison’s interest in Eastern instruments also shows on Sgt. Pepper’s “Within You Without You.” The Beatles brought ideas of transformation into performance; they went to India to study meditation with Maharishi Mahesh Yogi and pushed that into the mainstream. Remember: when we talk Beatles and Beach Boys we mean mainstream artists, not underground psychedelia. In summer 1967 Eastern culture as a source of wisdom met the West, and alternative spirituality truly fused with their music. Of course the Beatles did not stay psychedelic forever; they turned back. The White Album of November 1968 shows more of them as traditional songwriters, returning toward earlier ground. Its most ambitious piece is John Lennon’s tape piece “Revolution 9,” unlike most widely circulated electronic music in history. Many people hear it once and stop—or never finish—but it showed many that electronic music could sound like that.

What became Let It Be (planned as Get Back) finally appeared in the form of early 1969 sessions; that album returned to their roots. In September 1969 they released their last album, Abbey Road—perhaps their most fully psychedelic statement. Side one’s closer is “I Want You (She’s So Heavy)”: a crescendo of noise and repeating guitar chords that cuts off abruptly. On side two Paul strings many fragments into a suite. In this period the Beatles and Beach Boys, in a sense, injected more ambitious musical elements into the mainstream.

Next time we turn to San Francisco’s Haight-Ashbury psychedelic subculture and the growth of San Francisco radio—what was happening there at the same time.
